content: Antiretroviral drugs are effective in reducing the transmission of HIV from mothers to their infants by suppressing viral replication. This can be achieved either by lowering the maternal viral load during pregnancy or by providing post-exposure prophylaxis to the newborn. In high-income countries, the use of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), typically consisting of three drugs, has reduced mother-to-child transmission rates to approximately 1-2%. However, in lowand middle-income countries, where HAART may not be readily available, simpler and less expensive antiretroviral regimens have been implemented for pregnant women, their newborns, or both. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various antiretroviral regimens in reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and to assess their impact on maternal and infant mortality and morbidity. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing antiretroviral regimens to placebo, no treatment, or other regimens. Data were collected and analyzed to estimate the probability of HIV infection in infants at specific time points and to calculate the efficacy of the interventions. The review included 25 trials with a total of 18,901 participants. The trials varied in their design, with some randomizing mothers during pregnancy or labor and others randomizing infants. The first trial, conducted in 1991, compared zidovudine (ZDV) to placebo, and subsequent trials evaluated different drugs, dosages, and durations of treatment. Key Findings: 1. Antiretrovirals vs. Placebo in Breastfeeding Populations: ZDV administered to mothers from 36-38 weeks of gestation, during labor, and for 7 days postpartum significantly reduced HIV transmission at multiple time points, including 4-8 weeks (efficacy 32%), 6 months (efficacy 34.55%), and 18 months (efficacy 29.74%). ZDV combined with lamivudine (3TC) (PETRA regimen A) given to mothers from 36 weeks of gestation, during labor, and for 7 days postpartum, and to infants for 7 days after birth, significantly reduced HIV transmission at 4-8 weeks (efficacy 62.75%) but not at 18 months. Shorter regimens, such as ZDV plus 3TC given only during labor (PETRA regimen C), were not effective in reducing HIV transmission. 2. Antiretrovirals vs. Placebo in Non-Breastfeeding Populations: ZDV given to mothers from 14-34 weeks of gestation, during labor, and to infants for 6 weeks postpartum significantly reduced HIV transmission at 18 months (efficacy 66.22%). Shorter regimens, such as ZDV given from 36 weeks of gestation and during labor without infant treatment, were less effective. 3. Longer vs. Shorter Regimens Using the Same Antiretrovirals: In breastfeeding populations, longer ZDV regimens (starting at 36 weeks of gestation) did not show significant differences in HIV transmission rates compared to shorter regimens. In non-breastfeeding populations, longer ZDV regimens (starting at 28 weeks of gestation) were more effective than shorter regimens (starting at 35 weeks) in reducing HIV transmission at 6 months. 4. Regimens Using Different Drugs and Durations: A single dose of nevirapine (NVP) given to mothers during labor and to infants immediately after birth (HIVNET 012 regimen) was more effective than ZDV in reducing HIV transmission at multiple time points, including 18 months (efficacy 39.15%). Adding ZDV to the HIVNET 012 regimen for infants did not significantly improve outcomes. 5. Triple Antiretroviral Regimens (TRIPLE) vs. Other Regimens: In breastfeeding populations, a TRIPLE regimen initiated at 34 weeks of gestation showed no significant difference in HIV transmission rates compared to ZDV plus single-dose NVP at birth. In non-breastfeeding populations, a protease inhibitor-based TRIPLE regimen (lopinavir/ritonavir, ZDV, and 3TC) initiated at 26-34 weeks of gestation was more effective at 12 months in reducing HIV transmission compared to shorter ZDV-based regimens. 6. TRIPLE Regimen vs. TRIPLE Regimen: In breastfeeding populations, there was no significant difference in HIV transmission rates between two TRIPLE regimens (abacavir, lamivudine, and ZDV vs. lopinavir/ritonavir, ZDV, and lamivudine). Transmission rates were very low (<1%) in both groups. 7. Adverse Effects: Serious or life-threatening adverse events were not significantly different across the trials, suggesting that antiretroviral regimens are generally safe in the short term. Conclusions: Triple antiretroviral regimens are the most effective for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV. However, the optimal combination of drugs and the timing of initiation remain unclear. Short courses of antiretroviral drugs, such as ZDV combined with 3TC and single-dose NVP, are also effective and safe in the short term. For women presenting late in pregnancy, post-exposure prophylaxis with single-dose NVP and ZDV for 6 weeks postpartum is beneficial. The emergence of drug-resistant mutations, particularly with regimens containing NVP, requires further investigation to understand long-term implications.
